I have been intrigued on a number of occasions this session by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) lecturing the house about the importance of getting on with government business. Last Wednesday, for example, he rose and gave us a real tonguelashing because we dared to take up some of the time of the house in dealing with the munitions contract with the Janin company.
I have been wondering exactly what is government business this year. There are the trade agreements, for instance, and we have been accused of holding them up. Are they

On a point of order, sir; perhaps the leader of the opposition would be diffident about advancing this point himself, but one of the most widely accepted practices in the House of Commons is that the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition be given reasonable latitude when they are dealing with questions on the orders of the day or concerning the procedure of the house. The motion before the
house is that on and after Monday next government business shall have precedence over private members' resolutions. It is an extraordinary coincidence that the motion is made at the present time, because the opposition have had no resolutions so far. The time has been taken up largely with government business and motions by hon. members from other sections of the house. The motion at the head of page 12 of the order paper concerns any municipality in Canada, from Vancouver to Halifax. It is a motion relating to relief, municipal relief works and relief unemployment, There has been no declaration of policy on the part of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) as to what the government are going to do. The municipalities are now preparing their tax rates, but those rates cannot be struck until they know the policy of the government, which might be given in the discussion of this motion, which ordinarily would come up next Monday.
I want to direct attention to the rules of the house in this connection. If this motion is not discussed on a private members' day it remains on the order paper, and, by the rule of anticipation, it cannot be mentioned in this house on the estimates or at any other time. It is the most important resolution we have. What is to be done with these people who are on relief throughout Canada? In Ontario we get no help at all because the provincial government will not cooperate in the federal government's program of public works to relieve unemployment. It is true that the minister announced forty-forty-twenty as the

I have been in this house since 1921, and ever since that time motions of this kind have received a very wide interpretation. After all is said and done it must be remembered that the private member is the only connecting link between the government of the day and the electorate; and when he ceases to function this ceases to be a free parliament. A private member's resolution concerning unemployment, on the other hand, deals with the four or five hundred thousand oeople in Canada who are out of employment and who have stayed out of the penitentiaries. Therefore to my mind it is very much more important that we should deal with these people who are out of employment rather than with the people who are in the penitentiaries.
I should like to mention the other government measures which have been presented to the house, to show how important they are.
I have mentioned the amendments to the Penitentiaries Act. The next had to do with the appointment of auditors for the Canadian National Railways, a merely formal measure of no very great importance. The next dealt with the city of Ottawa agreement, under which $100,000 is granted the city of Ottawa, which is another annual statute. Then there were the amendments to the loan and trust companies acts, permitting these companies to allow their employees to enter into pension schemes. Then there was the Technical Education Act, a little more important, but not much. Then came the act to assess the owners of obstructions to the ascent or descent of fish such annual sums of money as the minister might determine. Fisheries are important; I do not wish to belittle them, but at the same time that was not a very important measure.
I have named, Mr. Speaker, about a dozen government measures, only one or two of which are of any importance at all. But what about the ones the government are holding up? What about the amendments to the Pension Act? What about the defence purchasing board? That is another measure that has been passed over day after day. Why is it being held up?
Let me show, on the other hand, what the private members have dealt with so far this session. We had the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Finn) bringing .up the loss of lobster traps and equipment on the western coast of Nova Scotia, certainly a very important matter from the point of view of the fishermen of that province. The hon. member for Wey-burn (Mr. Douglas) brought up the question of the distribution of seed wheat, an important matter for the prairies. Then there were the Bren gun contract and the Montreal construction company contract, both having to do with munitions and, as I have said, dealing with the $63,000,000 that is to be expended on defence this year. Yet those were the ones

I do not mean any disrespect to my hon. friend who brought up the question of the Canadian flag, but I think that was one of the least important subjects that could have been brought up at this time, with all our other problems. However, it is a matter of some importance.
Now I am going to give a list of a dozen private members' resolutions which remain on the order paper, almost any one of which to my mind is more important than any of the government business with which we have dealt thus far. I made up this list yesterday morning, and the first item is old age pensions, a matter which was discussed yesterday. Then comes unemployment and unemployment relief, which has to do with the four or five hundred thousand people in this country who are out of work. Surely that is a very important thing. Then there is a resolution having to do with a program of flood prevention and water conservation, brought in by one of my followers, the hon. member for Davenport, Toronto (Mr. MacNicol). There is a resolution dealing with the declaration of war by Canada; another concerning the stimulation of the sugar industry; another having to do with the encouragement of the use of Canadian coal; another regarding stabilized wheat prices; another advocating national control of the armament industry; another concerning the relief of youth unemployment; another having to do with the preservation of the halibut fisheries, and finally a resolution concerning national scholarships. I would say all these are very important; more so, I repeat, than practically any of the matters which have been brought up by the government thus far.
This talk, sir, by the leader of the government on three or four occasions to the effect that we were holding up the real business of the government, when they actually bring

in such unimportant measures as I have listed to-day, is one of the reasons why democracy is being discredited in this country. I do not think the right hon. gentleman had any right to complain of what he called holding up the business of the house. We have never done that. At all times he had 180 members behind him; at any time he could have moved an amendment and gone into government business, even on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, as he has done during the debate on the trade treaty. He could have done that at any time, unless he wished to abdicate his position as leader of this house. That is what the prime minister is, the leader of the house; and it is this bringing up of what to my mind are futile arguments of that sort against private members who are dealing with important subjects, while the government deals with unimportant subjects, that leads to the stirring up of feeling against democracy, to the leadership league of Mr. McCullagh and the new demagogism of Mr. Herridge. Those are the outgrowths of attempting to stifle public debate on important questions.
I say, sir, in closing, that so far as I am concerned I consider much of what the Prime Minister said on all these four times when he has got up and lectured the house about letting the government get on with public business is just so much claptrap and humbug. That is my opinion of most of what he has said about it. I challenge the government now to get down to business: to introduce, for example, legislation to deal with the great unemployment problem, or with the youth problem, or with national understanding, if you like, and with taxes and debt-to name only a few of the great problems. If he proceeds to deal with these important subjects, I think the right hon. gentleman would be well within his rights in asking the house to go on with government business, and for other hon. members to stop talking private resolutions. Until he does that, I think private members certainly have the edge on the argument, because the subjects with which their resolutions deal are very much more important than anything the Prime Minister has brought up thus far this session.

Before I do say a word in reply to what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) has said, may I assure hon. members that the procedure which the government is following this session is not different from that which has been followed in other sessions, nor is it any less generous but rather more generous towards
private members' resolutions. May I give to hon. members the number of Mondays which have elapsed between the opening and the dates on which Mondays have been taken as government days. In the session of 1932-33 five Mondays had elapsed; in the session of 1934, five; in 1935, four; in 1936, five; in 1937, three; in 1938, six, and this year eight Mondays have elapsed.
I would point out the relative importance of government business and the business of private members, because I hold, notwithstanding what the leader of the opposition has said, that after all, government business is more important than private members' resolutions, however important they may be. The government is the body responsible for carrying on the business of the country, and it is the best judge of what that business is. But in order that hon. members may not imagine that most of the Mondays since the opening were taken up with the debate on the address and other debates which have been mentioned, may I place on record the number of Mondays actually given up to private members' business. In the session of 1932-33 there were four Mondays; in 1934, four; in 1935, three; in 1936, four; in 1937, two; in 1938. four, and in 1939, five. This session, therefore, more Mondays have been given to private members than have been given in any of the sessions since 1932. I mention these figures because they show that in every way the government has been considerate of the rights of private members.
My hon. friend has talked about the different measures we might have gone on with. May I point out that in the debate on the address I mentioned the first measure which would be taken up as a government measure would be the trade treaty with the United States. We regard that as a very important piece of legislation. I may say I do not think a more important piece of legislation has been introduced to this parliament at any time, unless it was the treaty of three years ago, of which in part this is a continuation and in part an addition. At any rate I made that announcement at that time so that hon. members would not feel it necessary when speaking in the debate on the address in reply to take up their time in discussing matters which would relate to the trade treaty. I wanted to give them the assurance at once that they would have that opportunity when the debate on the address was over.
I thought by giving that assurance we might shorten the debate on the address. I have given one reason why the government decided to proceed next with the trade treaty.

But there was another reason, and a special one, why the government made the trade treaty the first important measure of the session. It was this: As hon. members well know, when the debate on the resolution respecting the trade treaty is completed we will then have to go into committee of ways and means to discuss the various items in the schedule. I imagine the discussion of those items will take a considerable time. Following the discussion of the items in committee of ways and means we will have to introduce a bill, the three stages of which will have to be passed by the house, including again discussions in the committee of ways and means. All that will take a considerable length of time.
I think it will be to the interest of hon. members in the house and to the country that the budget should be brought down as early this year as possible. Hon. members will know the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) can hardly undertake to get his budget in shape for presentation until this all-important measure, the trade agreement with the United States is out of the way.
I say that is the reason why at the outset we gave the right of way to the trade treaty. We knew it would take considerable time to get the measure through, so that the path might be cleared for the Minister of Finance to bring in his budget at this session at as early a date as possible.
My hon. friend has spoken about some of the lesser measures which have been on the order paper. Among the number he referred to the penitentiaries bill, which is now before us. What was said about the penitentiaries bill at the end of the last session by many who were critical of the government at that time, and by no one more strongly than by the leader of the opposition in another house, when the measure was in that place? It was stated that the penitentiaries measure was one of the most important that any government could bring forward, but that we had left it to the very end of the session, and that therefore there was not the opportunity to discuss it in the detail which its importance merited. Well, the best answer to a criticism of that kind is to make a measure of that sort one of the very first pieces of business after the opening of the session. We do attach very considerable importance to the penitentiaries measure, notwithstanding the fact that the leader of the opposition has different views concerning it. The reason for bringing it up at this time is to permit it to be sent to the other house at as early a moment as possible, so that there may be no excuse, so far as the discussions in that place

are concerned, of its not having been presented in ample time. There have been some small measures, but they have taken very little of the time of the house. Time has been taken up with the debate on the address, with the debate with respect to defence contracts, with the Bren gun resolution and with the resolution moved the other day to refer another munitions contract to the public accounts committee. The remainder of the time has been taken up largely with the discussion of the trade treaty. As I have said, it was felt the smaller measures would not take up much time. It was thought advisable to have some of these measures sent to the other house so that they would be available for the consideration of members there when they assembled again, which I believe they are to do to-day. If these smaller measures, if you wish to so describe them, had not been brought forward, there would not have been as much in the way of legislation for immediate consideration in the other house as will now be the case.
The real occasion of delay this session has been the discussion with regard to the two contracts of the defence department. My criticism with respect to that discussion has been, not that there should not be full and ample discussion with respect to these particular measures or with respect to all measures affecting the department of defence, but that there is a time and place for all things. The time and place to discuss these contracts was in the committee of public accounts after they had been referred to the committee and again in this house after the committee had reported. If there had been any objection to referring them, then there would have been ample ground for opposition and discussion, but when the government was ready to refer them, the discussion that took place was I think completely unwarranted in the circumstances.
The leader of the opposition says that we have held back certain legislation. He referred to one measure which was important and which he says should have come on before this, the resolution with respect to the setting up of a defence purchasing board. That resolution was placed on the order paper on February 7, just a month ago. The intention of the government was to bring in the measure with respect to the defence purchasing board the minute we were through with the trade agreement, which we regarded as being the most important measure of all. That has been our intention all along. There would have been ample opportunity during the debate on that measure to discuss all questions relating to contracts of the defence depart-

Precedence for Government Business
ment and hon. members knew that when they were debating the motions to refer specific contracts to the public accounts committee. The house chose to discuss those particular references when we might have been going on with government business had we not been thus precluded. We regarded the resolution to set up a defence purchasing board as one of great importance and the only reason why we have not been able to reach this measure before this is the amount of time that has been taken up in discussing other measures, including the two motions respecting a reference of defence contracts to the committee of public accounts.
Let me say this in passing with regard to some of the discussion that has taken place. I do not share the view which seems to be held in some quarters that parliament should cease to be a deliberative assembly, that it is not necessary to have the government informed by hon. members from different parts of Canada of the conditions existing in their constituencies and in their parts of the country or to have public opinion moulded in a deliberative and careful way. I regard parliament as being essentially a forum in which progress can best be made by reasoned discussion, not by snap-hasty judgment and quick decision without any opportunity of weighing the merits of measures pro and con. I regard it as being the one great bulwark that is left to a free democracy to-day, and left only to those countries where parliamentary institutions still exist. These free institutions have been wiped out largely in most parts of the world, but the essence of our parliamentary system of government is the opportunity it affords to discuss very fully the pros and cons of what has taken place or is taking place in each part of the country. Hon. members should be allowed to talk frankly and freely with respect to conditions as they know them in different parts of the country.
My hon. friend has mentioned the discussion of unemployment and other problems. I wonder how a greater facility could have been afforded by the government to every hon. member to discuss unemployment than was afforded during the debate on the address? Hon. members took ample advantage of that opportunity and they gave to the administration their views with regard to the situation as it existed in their parts of the country. There are going to be further opportunities. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition made another extraordinary remark. He said that he did not think that supply was of much concern, that it was something that came up on Friday nights to fill in. I have always thought that the voting of supply was
one of the most important of all the functions of parliament. Without supply being voted government itself cannot be carried on. Moreover when supply is being discussed is the time above all times when hon. members have an opportunity to discuss anything they wish, to take up any concrete problem, to discuss any matter of public importance and to take part in debate to an extent which is not afforded to them in like measure at other times. As my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has just mentioned to me, there is not a single resolution on the order paper the main features of which could not be discussed very fully, either when the government was going into supply or when the house was in committee of supply.
The leader of the opposition probably is somewhat new to his office, but if he had the duty of leading the house-I do not think it is at all probable he is likely to have-he would then find that these matters had to be thought out. not as he is accustomed to doing by quick reasoning and snap judgment but rather by looking ahead in connection with the business of the country generally. I see my hon. friend is looking at me rather sharply. I do not know whether I have said something which has offended him. However, he has said something this afternoon to which I wish to refer more particularly.
The leader of the opposition said that I had sought to alarm parliament by talking about war. I do not think any hon. member will find the word "war" mentioned in anything I have said. I did say that I thought there were more important matters which we might be called upon to consider at almost any time and that we would do well to get on with the work of the house. I suppose there is no more difficult position in which a leader of a government can be placed than to know just how far it is advisable to go in warning members of parliament or the country of a situation as it exists, or how far it is wise to remain silent.
I remember last September that members of the Conservative party in this country were pretty strong in their attacks upon myself. They said that knowing that a situation which was coming along was going to be very critical, I should have taken the country more into my confidence and told the people to be prepared for an emergency. As I say, it is a very difficult position in which a leader of an administration is sometimes placed, because one has great responsibility. However, there are ways of seeking to meet it. While one cannot always take the entire house into his confidence, parliament has provided a means of courtesy whereby the leader of the

Precedence for Government Business
government, should he regard a situation as being serious, may call in the leader of the opposition. I did that with my hon. friend the leader of the opposition since this house opened this year. Some dispatches which I was receiving were of so serious a nature that my colleagues and I felt that they ought to be shown to the leader of the opposition. I asked him if he would come to my room and allow me to show him what the government and I had received with respect to conditions as they were developing in Europe, and what we must be prepared for in the event of matters taking a certain turn. How my hon. friend, in the light of the information he then had, could chide me this afternoon for having made the remark that I did the other day to hon. members with respect to hurrying on with business because we might have some more important matters to consider, I have yet to understand. I say to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition that I question very much if he would have wished to receive dispatches which were more serious than those which I showed to him. Since I showed him the dispatches I did, I have received others, perhaps a little less serious, but nevertheless of a character to cause the government to view with great concern matters which were happening in other parts of the world. I am happy to say that, more particularly in the last day or two, the skies seem to have cleared very considerably. During the earlier period it was still doubtful how the civil war in Spain would end: in all the capitals of Europe there was, I believe, very great fear as to how the situation might develop over the whole of Europe. But certainly, since that situation has cleared up to the extent it has, there has been very great relief in, I believe, all the foreign offices of Europe. I cannot say more than that. I am not going to seek to influence in any way the judgment of this house. What I said the other day I still adhere to as something which I think it was proper I should have given to hon. members, all the circumstances considered.
I might go on and speak of the importance of some other measures, and let me just add this. I have never known an administration to place all of its important legislation on the order paper at once. I have noticed, following business in this parliament during the years I have been in it, that the invariable practice has been not to begin except for special reasons with the most important measures but with some of the minor measures until parliament, so to speak, got under way with its work. Apart from that, the fact that the government has not been holding back 
important measures is evidenced by the order paper itself, which contains more than one bill that my hon. friend the leader of the opposition says is important. I might add to those mentioned the bill to amend the Pensions Act. That bill has been on the order paper since January 18. The measure I have mentioned, to create a defence purchasing board, has been on the order paper since February 7. Another important bill, a measure of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, has stood there since February 10. and the resolution with respect to the loan under the consolidated revenue act has been on the paper since February 3. It is simply childish to speak about the government's business not being important because the order paper is not laden up with measures which there is no possibility of reaching at the present time, and which would be kept there and called day after day, taking up space on the order paper and the time of parliament in the calling of measures which it is known cannot be reached for some little time to come. I hold that the government has evidenced full circumspection as respects both the business of the house and the consideration shown private members. I am not surprised, however, that my friend the leader of the opposition, feels it necessary to seek to make out some sort of case for himself and his following with respect to the amount of time they have been responsible for wasting this session.

His tactics are to draw a red herring across the trail. That is what he did the other day with regard to this supposedly terribly critical world situation-a situation no more critical than it has been for months and months, but he knew that by so doing he would distract attention from the fact that he had not given any answer to the question whether he supported the idea of giving to pets and favourites of the government these high-priced munitions contracts.

1932-33, after the empire conference at Ottawa, when there had been a very important agreement which might be compared to the one that is before the house at the present time. On that occasion the session was called earlier for the purpose of having parliament ratify that agreement. As a matter of fact we were called to meet on October 6, 1932, and on October 12 the then prime minister moved the ratification of that agreement. The house sat continuously discussing the agreement and the division on the third reading took place on November 22. The house discussed the agreement continuously, and, as I have said, the session had been called earlier for that purpose. Now, however, we find that the house has been in session almost two months, since the beginning of January. The trade treaty is not even in committee; it is being discussed on the resolution. We have not been able to make any progress with it.
I agree with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) when he protests against the comments of those outside the house who claim that parliament is doing nothing when discussing the trade agreement. Those leadership leaguers should understand that on very important business such as this, parliament not only has the right but it has the duty to discuss everything that is relevant-and that is doing the business of the country. When members of the house are discussing the treaty they are doing the business of the country, and it is therefore useless to publish a blank space and indicate underneath that parliament has done nothing. Surely, however, an end must be reached in the discussion of the trade treaty as well as in any other discussion, and I say with all due deference to my hon. friend that while he protests against the statements of Mr. McCullagh and the other gentleman who criticized parliament about the business that is being carried on, he gives them material by helping to some extent to prevent the business of the house being done.

Supply, the voting of money for public business, is the main work of parliament, and as the Prime Minister has said, with respect to every one of the resolutions on the order paper, the subject involved may be discussed in supply. ^Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport): Yesterday the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) asked me to make a statement with reference to any changes in the collection of radio licence fees. Having looked over the

file I find a letter addressed to myself from J. R. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST VANCOUVER IN GRAIN SHIPMENTS
speechtext: I wish to address a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler). According to a news item appearing in the Vancouver Province of March 2, a direct charge has been made by the mayor of Vancouver that the dominion government, through the wheat board, has discriminated against Vancouver by ordering grain shipments to move east instead of west. In view of the seriousness of the matter to the Pacific coast ports, I think some statement should be made by the minister.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. D. EULER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION AGAINST VANCOUVER IN GRAIN SHIPMENTS
speechtext: I should like to make my reply to that question just as emphatic as possible. Perhaps it is unnecessary to say that the government never at any time interferes with the operations of the wheat board, either with regard to purchases or sales or the manner in which the wheat shall go forward to the markets of the world. I asked the chairman of the board as to this charge and he says that there is absolutely no favouritism in regard to routing the grain, that it is routed eastward or westward according as it is to the financial interest of the board and of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
If my hon. friend refers to the new system we want to inaugurate, the guards who will be appointed by the commission will have to undergo training and will be appointed only after their qualifications have been fully approved and recognized. Then they will be given the opportunity to show their capacity, their character, their ability to manage, and so on, and the intention is that deputy wardens and wardens will be appointed from among the men who have made good in the various services of the penitentiaries.
Up to the present nothing of this kind has existed. I know how difficult it has been in the past for ministers of justice to find the best possible men to put at the head of the various penitentiaries. When men already in the service could be appointed, after they had proved that they could assume the responsibility, they usually were appointed. Otherwise it is a difficult task for the authorities to find the best available men. As a matter of fact at the present time there are one or two vacancies, and I have the various officers of the department at work trying to find the best possible men to appoint. I believe that with the system which will be organized it will be possible to obtain trained men. It is even the intention to have a training school under the commission-of

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: I should like to say a few words in opposition to the procedure adopted by the government with respect to this section. The government has decided to appoint a commission, responsible to the minister and parliament, to administer the penitentiaries. The other day, speaking to the committee, the minister said, in effect, that when appointed the committee would be composed of individuals in whom the people of Canada could have complete confidence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext: That is my hope.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
And that they would not be selected because of political bias. I am sure every hon. member appreciates that statement, and I believe the commission will be as the minister has suggested. In my opinion no one should have a greater desire than the minister that the commission be composed of men of the best possible type. But it seems to me the government is making a mistake when, after appointing a commission responsible to the government, it then undertakes to appoint wardens, deputy wardens and other administrative or executive officers who must operate under the commission. I suggest that the appointment of the wardens, and the wardens only, might be left with the commission. As the commission is responsible to the government for the administration of the penitentiaries I think it should be permitted to select the persons directly under it. But w'ith the exception of the wardens, all the other employees in the penitentiaries should be appointed by the civil service commission.
I see no reason why we should set up a civil service commission and then leave appointments to other persons. Let me quote the words of the present Prime Minister on this subject, when he was leader of the opposition. On March 30, 1933, the then leader of the opposition was speaking to a resolution which had been introduced by the former minister of justice with respect to the appointment of penitentiary officials by the governor in council, a provision similar to that now before the committee. The right hon. gentleman is reported in Hansard for 1032-33 at page 3544, as follows:
Mr. Speaker, this resolution involves the introduction of a bill which means a departure from the merit system and a return to the discredited patronage system with respect to appointments in connection with the penitentiaries of our country. In a word, it will make 71492-103
political machines out of the penitentiaries, and I want therefore to take very strong exception, at the very outset, to the passage of this resolution.
I submit that that is strong language from the present Prime Minister. But he went farther, and said:
To begin with it will have an unsettling effect upon the whole civil service of Canada. If this important branch of the civil service is to he withdrawn from the operation of the Civil Service Act, and the control of the Civil Service Commission, it will be but the thin edge of the wedge, the introduction, in other words, of a policy on the part of the administration to withdraw other services from the control of the Civil Service Act. Hon. gentlemen opposite were in office. I believe, at the time provisions of the Civil Service Act were extended to cover some of the outside services, and they will recollect the difficulty there was in getting the measure through the house and the necessity of backing up their efforts by strong public opinion throughout Canada.
And then he goes on:
I said that before, some time ago, and what has happened since bears out the truth of my statement. That a group of gentlemen, none of whom has any special training or the expert knowledge required in determining the qualifications of a warden of a penitentiary, should undertake such appointments, is a course of procedure certainly open to question.
It is only fair to add that with respect to the appointment of wardens he went on to
say:
All things considered I believe that concerning important technical positions requiring certain special personal and other qualifications, the minister himself is perhaps better able than the commission to make appointments. ... I just wish to stress at the outset what has been recognized by the press of all political parties since the resolution appeared on the order paper to be a distinct step backwards and a great misfortune. I was hoping the minister was going to allow the resolution to remain on the order paper until the close of the session, since it had been there already for so long a time.
I believe the leader of the opposition of that day was on strong ground. It is my opinion that this government would be making a mistake if it were to adopt the section as it now stands.
As I said before, I believe the appointment of wardens should be left to the commission, but that deputy wardens, other administrative or executive officers and all other employees in the penitentiaries should be appointed by the civil service commission. I hope the minister will take these points into consideration before the bill receives third reading, with a view to bringing in an amendment along these lines.

hon. friend and members of the committee

Penitentiaries Commission

I am responsible for what happens in the
fenitentiaries of Canada at the present time.
am responsible if there are evasions; 1 am responsible if there is a rebellion in a penitentiary anywhere; and I think it is not fair that the wardens and the deputy wardens, the main officers, and even the guards in the penitentiaries, should be selected under a system of [DOT]competitive examination. It is absurd. I think that penitentiary work should be compared with the work of the mounted police or even of the militia. In the penitentiary the work that is to be done by the guards, and very often their lives are in jeopardy, depends for its success more on the character and the temperament of the man than on what they may happen to know about geography or arithmetic or anything else. This conviction I have formed during the year and a half in which I have been at the head of the administration of the Department of Justice. I believe in control by the Civil Service Commission when it is a case of appointments in connection with ordinary departmental work, but I do not think they are qualified to select the men to conduct the penitentiaries.
Up until 1930 while I was Minister of Justice no change was made in the system of appointments. Three years after he had taken charge of the department, my predecessor in office, Hon. Mr. Guthrie, introduced legislation for the purpose of taking away from the civil service commission the appointments to the penitentiaries. That is the law as it exists to-day. My hon. friend has read what the then leader of the opposition said, but he should also read my words when I spoke on that bill. I supported the bill because I thought Mr. Guthrie was right in taking charge of the appointments to the penitentiaries. This is work of a special character, comparable to the work of the mounted police, or even the army. However, I objected to that part of the bill which dealt with the stenographers and clerks employed in the branch, and Mr. Guthrie agreed to change the bill and not apply its provisions to those engaged in clerical work. If my hon. friend turns to page 3652 of the Hansard from which he has just read, he will find that my leader agreed with what I had stated. He approved the bill as it referred to wardens, deputy wardens and those in charge of convicts in the penitentiaries.
One has only to consider the matter to realize that this is not something which could be done by the civil service commission. As I said the other day, the Minister of

Justice is responsible when things go wrong in that difficult branch of the department. Under the new system which I want to establish, the permanent officers will have to go through a training period, as I told the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol). They will then become specialized in their work and the prison commission will be in charge of appointments. The appointment of wardens and deputy wardens will be kept under the governor in council, but no appointment will be made without the recommendation of the commission. I would have no objection to adding those words to section 10 if it is thought desirable that they should be added.

speechtext:
I feel disposed to support the clause, having heard the minister say that the intention of the department is to follow the custom now followed in the
Penitentiaries Commission

old country. I suppose it will take some little time to work it out. I am now going to speak of it as it has been in operation. I took particular interest in it while I was at Leeds, and also-and particularly-at Bar-linnie prison, at Glasgow. The acting warden then in charge at Barlinnie had been deputy warden at Wakefield, and during his term of office at Wakefield had been in charge of the [DOT] school. I went to particular pains to learn how the appointments were made, and whether they were in any way political, and he assured me that so far as he knew they were absolutely non-political. If a position becomes vacant in any prison, the authorities-I assume, the home office-are notified at once. Having ascertained that a position is to be filled, the home office would then communicate, as I understood, with the person in charge of the school.
Although I may be wrong, not being very familiar with that kind of administration, the inference I drew was that the appointments were wholly non-political, made on recommendation of the authorities at Wakefield, and from the school at Wakefield officers were sent hither and thither to all the prisons of England. If I am in error in that assumption perhaps the minister can correct me. If that system is followed I cannot see that there is anything political about appointments. That is what the deputy warden told me: he got his own appointment without any political pull. He had no politics; he had been trained in the school, graduated therefrom, obtained a position and worked his way up in a certain number of years to be deputy warden of one of the chief prisons of the old country. Personally I am strong for civil service commission control, but I do not see how it could control this. speechtext:
When the hon. member
for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) compares the civil service in Great Britain with the civil service in Canada he is comparing two things which are not comparable, because political patronage has entirely disappeared from the *civil service in Great Britain. Sir Francis Floud, when he appeared before the civil service committee last year, made the statement in answer to a question that a recommendation from a member of parliament would be IMr. MacNicol.]
an obstacle rather than an aid to the securing of a position in the civil service. This afternoon we heard a minister say that appointments in a certain department were to be made on the recommendation not of a member of parliament but of a candidate who had been defeated, in whom the electors of the constituency had showed they had no confidence. He is the person who in certain cases will make appointments. It was drawn to my attention last year in the house that the recommendation of an hon. member in another province carried far more weight than that of the elected member in the constituency in which the appointment was to be made. I heard the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail) say that this could not be done under the civil service commission. There was a civil service committee appointed in 1921. An attempt was made at that time to take some of these classes from under the civil service commission, and the then superintendent of penitentiaries, General W. S. Hughes, was a witness before the committee. In reply to a query by a cabinet minister as to whether he would prefer to have the selections made by the civil service commission rather than by himself, General Hughes said:
I would prefer they would do it, very much.
Q. Why?
A. Under the system in which they appoint them, it gives our warden practically full control over them, because it gives our warden an opportunity to see whether they are satisfactory to him or not, and if they are not he has only to let them go. Under the old system, if we were saddled with a bad man we would have to keep him. We had no power to dismiss him.
I am not saying that the minister would interfere with the dismissal of a man whom the commission found unsatisfactory, and I am not saying that if we had the machinery they have developed in Great Britain for these appointments, the suggestions made would not be all to the good. But we have not that machinery. Political appointments are made in all departments, and unless we provide that these appointments shall be made by the civil service commission, they will continue to be made politically, no matter what the minister or anyone else may say.

Perhaps

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
The whole plan of this reform for the control of these institutions hinges on the principle involved in subsections 1 and 2 of section 10. It seems to me we are getting merely the form and not the substance of real prison reform. In the first place the key men in the penitentiaries will be those appointed by the commission. The men who will actually be in control of human beings are to be appointed by the commission. On the other hand, we have the governor in council, and the governor in council is always regarded as a political agency. I do not say
that it will be so in respect of the present Minister of Justice, but under section 10 the appointment will be made by the governor general in council on the recommendation of the commission. The commission will be a lot of figureheads with power merely to recommend the heads and chiefs. Who are the key men the governor in council appoints? They are the wardens, deputy wardens and other administrative officers, including, I suppose, teachers and medical officers, bookkeepers and technical men. They are to be appointed by the government on recommendation of the commission. The governor in council will be in Ottawa, the commission will be in Ottawa, while the men really at the head of the institution will be on the scene of battle. In my opinion the proposal before us will lead to inefficiency, lack of responsibility, divided control and lack of proper supervision of these institutions.
The 800 men in Kingston penitentiary, for example, will be regulated and drilled by officers appointed by the commission. In other words, you will have an agency up here appointing key men whose duty it will be to maintain control over 800 men in that institution. It seems to me that the whole bill is top heavy and will soon be on its way to be upside down. I have had a great deal of experience with commissions of various kinds and J know very well what difficulties and complications are going to be met with under this bill when the commission is set up. Mr. Brockington was before a radio committee of the house the other day and he intimated that he was beyond the control of parliament and could do as he liked over the head of parliament. In the same way, if you pass section 10 of this bill, you can say good-bye to any further control by parliament of our penal institutions for the next twenty-five years, and we who sit here will be responsible twenty years from now if we find by that time there has been no progress or no substantial reform has been introduced. The same policy that has been pursued in connection with the radio commission, the railway commission and similar bodies will operate here, and you will find that this commission will be top heavy. It is going to be a sort of regular standing army with its key men, guards, teachers, mechanics and others who will be actually in charge of the inmates, and to these commissioners we are going to hand over powers which we have never dreamed of giving to our judges. These officers will be able to make rules and regulations which even a judge presiding outside in a
Penitentiaries Commission

court of justice cannot promulgate, and to give to these rules and regulations the force of statutes.
The policy itself has been condemned by the court of appeal of the province. Without this parliament's knowledge or consent, these officers and warden's courts may extend a man's term and impose penalties which even the judge who sentenced the prisoner had not the power to impose. Yet we sit here handing over to a commission of this sort the power to appoint a certain class of men to these important positions. It reminds me of Coxey's army, with all the array of brass hats. Everybody of importance will be a general or a brigadier or a brass hat, appointed by the governor in council. When it comes to the men on the ground, the captains, the lieutenants, the sergeants and the corporals, they will be appointed by some gentlemen known as the commission; and when any trouble arises in the * west one of the commissioners, I presume, will travel with a staff and retinue, all over the country, just as if he were in the army, and with no results.
Nothing is said in this bill about reclamation and prevention. We all know what prevention in hygiene and medicine and public health have done; yet in this most important piece of legislation dealing with such an important problem, no provision is being made to reclaim the inmates of our penitentiaries or to prevent crime, nor are there any'prevention measures in it. The hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. McCann) the other day spoke words of wisdom when he discussed certain conditions in our penitentiaries. He dealt with the social and medical problem in its relation to public health, and what he had to say in that regard might well be heeded by the minister. The minister is a gentleman in whom I have the utmost confidence and whom I respect, and I would rather see him in control. Let him appoint the superintendent and the other important officers himself and retain control. I think it would be far better. In England the Home Secretary has a central board, and he gives these people a free hand. This section may have been drafted by lawyers, but you are just divesting yourself forever of any authority.

I suggest that the new section 45 is, with the exception of a few words, the same as the present section 40. These institutions have certain privileged visitors who rarely visit. Rightly or wrongly, these institutions are managed by the crown, and I say there should be some proper public and independent inspection of penitentiaries by grand juries.
The late Chief Justice Meredith presided at the assizes in Ontario for over forty years. Speaking to a grand jury in the county of York in 1930, he made reference to a bill which was before this house seven or eight years ago and which gave power to the grand jury to make public inspection. Reading the amendment to the grand jury he said, in effect, that federal and provincial institutions, whether rightly or wrongly managed, are managed by the crown, and grand juries as representatives of the public should during a period of the assize courts have the right to visit any of those institutions in the town where the assizes are held. They would obtain their authority from the judge presiding at an assize court.
That privilege has been in existence in England for years. Over there the grand or

Penitentiaries Commission

other jury insists upon inspection of institutions. Under the provincial system a grand jury visited an asylum and found several sane men in it. Yet there were officials of all kinds in that province. Although there is inspection by the officials mentioned in the section, in my humble opinion many of them are just figureheads, and they do not make a public inspection. It is no inspection at all.
The late Chief Justice Meredith was on circuit work for forty years, and was one of the ablest judges who has ever served in Ontario. He wondered why the principle of inspection, one which has been found in the British criminal law for many years, could not be carried out here. The section under discussion provides for certain visitors. There may be visits when the officials know you are coming. Those visitors will come by train, bring their aides-de-camp, and all that sort of thing. Under those circumstances they will learn a lot, won't they! But if a grand jury were permitted to make a visit, I suggest it would not interfere with the discipline of the institution or cause any expense. If we had had that system years ago, the deplorable conditions which are described in the report would not have existed. We learn of juveniles of sixteen years of age in those institutions, and practices which are opposed to all the known principles of proper dealing with the unfortunate.
In my opinion the minister should be prepared to accept an amendment to the bill permitting a visit from a grand jury. I see no reason why his officials should oppose such legislation. That just shows how much reform one can expect under this new commission, when the department will not accept the principle of the law of England whereby they have a central board, and further the principle whereby a grand or other jury may visit these institutions. These institutions are under the control of the crown, and the crown may do what it likes in connection with them. There are warden's courts within the jurisdiction of the institutions, and they may pass rules and regulations with which even this parliament would not have power to interfere. Yet we are denied the privilege of adding grand juries to the list of visitors.

The causes of delinquency outside the home are mostly to be found in the character of the street and neighbourhood in which the child lives. subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT SWEEPSTAKES ORGANIZED BY PROVINCES FOR BENEFIT OF UNIVERSITIES OR HOSPITALS

speechtext:
Mr. VITAL MALLETTE (Jacques-Cartier) moved the second reading of Bill No. 10, to amend the criminal code.
He said:	Hon. members will no doubt
remember that this same bill was introduced at the 1938 session by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Bertrand). They will also remember that an interesting discussion followed; that great interest was taken in that bill by the people of Canada; that newspapers referred to it upon numerous occasions, that a considerable amount of correspondence was directed to the members upon its merits; but that, alas, no vote was taken on it and the session was concluded without the House of Commons and the Senate having an opportunity of expressing their approval or otherwise of this important measure. This lack
Criminal Code-Sweepstakes

of a decision last year renders it necessary that the bill be reintroduced this year, and its sponsor of 1938, having to go to England this winter, could not present the bill himself owing to the uncertainties of the day and hour when he could perform the task. Since I had strongly supported the bill last year, he asked me to take charge of it on this occasion, a request to which I readily acceded.
The arguments advanced last session in favour of this amendment to the criminal code are just as good this year. They have not been weakened in any way whatever. The hospitals and universities in Canada are still in need of funds. Without going into details, let me just remind hon. members that the usual campaigns in aid of charities were held last fall; the needs of these worthy institutions were just as great and pressing as previously, and there is no sign on the horizon indicating an improvement in that situation.
Just as I did in last year's debate, I wish to pay a tribute of deep admiration and gratitude to the thousands of generous people who have helped our universities and hospitals, doctors, nurses and others on hospital staffs, the staffs of the universities, and those great silent workers of the religious congregations whose self-forgetful devotion to their fellow-men and women is beyond description, beyond appreciation and beyond adequate recognition. In spite of the help generously extended ,by benefactors great and small, in spite of the support and cooperation given by the public, and in spite of the sacrifices cheerfully made by those noble souls in charge of such institutions, there is still a financial gap to bridge.
A plight of this sort is not, I assume, limited to Canada. It is not a purely local trouble. But even if other countries encounter the same difficulty, that does not improve conditions in Canada. While we are not conversant with the means taken by other countries to correct this unfortunate condition, we are aware that one country holds a public lottery called sweepstakes, for the benefit of its hospitals. That country is Eire, formerly known as the Irish Free State. We know also that tickets for these sweepstakes are sold in Canada, notwithstanding the prohibition contained in our criminal code against their sale. Let me ask whether or not we consider as criminals those of our friends and acquaintances who purchase such tickets. Of course not. I admit that some of the buyers of these tickets are possibly little interested in the hospitals themselves and buy the tickets as a sporting chance in
£Mr. Mallette.]
the hope of winning something. Nevertheless the fact remains that they do buy these tickets, the prohibition notwithstanding, and therefore whatever money is risked in that way is lost to Canada and Canadian institutions. Should we not admire the wisdom and sagacity of those Irish gentlemen who understand human nature well enough to capitalize upon one of its little weaknesses and turn it to the advantage of charity-because that is precisely what happens through the operation of sweepstakes in aid of Irish hospitals. Those Irish gentlemen, with that keenness and kindness which are foremost among the many fine qualities of the Irish people, saw an opportunity of reaping benefits for the hospitals in that country in the hope of profit that lies dormant in the minds of most men and women who are prepared to take a chance. They saw that opportunity and cleverly took advantage of it. The response has been tremendous. Why should we not do the same for Canada? The answer is in the hands, or, rather, in the votes of the members of this house and the senate.
In case some hon. members are under the impression that sweepstake tickets are not sold in Canada, I quote for their information the heading of a news item that appeared in the Ottawa Journal of March 25, 1938, which reads:
64-year-old miller in Kenora wins $150,000.
Further down, referring to sweepstakes, the article itself says:
Buyers paid $13,730,010 for their chances to get rich quick.
Winners were paid a total of $8,057,600. That left a balance of $5,672,410.
I have here also an extract from La Presse of Montreal of August 16, 1938, giving a list of the winners of what they call the sole Canadian sweepstakes. They refer to the Dominion Rifle Association sweepstakes. People wonder why this sweepstake is allowed and others are not.
Again, I have here an article that appeared in La Patrie of October 23, 1938, which states:
Eight hundred Canadians have won consolation prizes in the Irish sweepstake.
There is a given list which is too long to insert in this speech, and anyway it has no bearing on my argument.
Without wishing to be personal, I believe that if I were to send a questionnaire to hon. members requesting information as to their investments of this kind for, say each year during the last ten years, the replies would be interesting provided the whole truth were told-and that from lawmakers, notwithstanding the law prohibiting the sale of such

Criminal Code-Sweepstakes
tickets. However, I will not perpetrate such a cruelty. Why should a law which is not respected, which is not obeyed and which is not advantageous to the country, be kept on the statute books?
This bill provides that such sweepstakes be permitted only when organized by the government of a province by or under a law of the legislature of such province. Any provinces that do not want to permit such sweepstakes do not have to. Where a province desires to do so, the adoption of a bill will allow the legal holding of sweepstakes. The people of Quebec, I am sure, favour the present bill, and I hope that hon. members from other provinces will give their opinion due consideration inasmuch as the holding of sweepstakes would be optional. No province would be bound to hold them, and that in itself is a valid reason for the adoption of this bill, because it would permit the willing provinces to hold sweepstakes, while it would not compel unwilling provinces to act. Surely that is a fair interpretation of British fair play.
As an example, some twenty years ago a great wave of sentiment swept over most of north America in favour of prohibition, in the hope of achieving total abstinence from the use of alcoholic liquors. The leaders of the movement were undoubtedly sincere in their ambition, and if they had succeeded the world would be different from what it is today. But they counted without allowing for human nature, and every hon. member knows the results. At that time, when governments were falling over one another in the rush to adopt prohibitory legislation, there was one Canadian province which stood aloof, the province of Quebec, home of good, sound common sense. Its government knew that nowhere can men and women be made or kept good just by passing laws. The government of Quebec adopted at that time state control of the sale of alcoholic liquors, and that policy has since been copied everywhere in Canada and even beyond our frontiers. I cite this example, in case hon. members may think this demand to legalize the sale and purchase of sweepstake tickets might be as far as Quebec is concerned a mere whim.
I have a better proof here than just my own opinion. On April 20, 1934, a law was assented to in the Quebec legislature entitled "An act to authorize the organizing of a lottery for education and public charitable purposes." At the end it states:
The power given to the lieutenant-governor in council by section 1 shall be exercised only if a lottery of the nature of that contemplated by this act is not prohibited by statute of the parliament of Canada.
Moreover such power shall not be exercised if the parliament of Canada authorizes the Canadian government to organize a general lottery in the whole of Canada for purposes similar to those contemplated by the preceding provisions.
And those purposes were recited in clause 2, which reads:
The proceeds from the lottery, after deducting the amounts fixed for the prizes and those required to pay the expenses of organization and of selling of tickets and other incidental expenses, as well as the salaries of the officers and employees appointed under section 3, must be employed exclusively for educational or public charitable purposes carried on in the province and designated by the lieutenant-governor in council.
I wish to add that one of the important political parties in Quebec, L'Action Liberale Nationale, has in its platform a clause approving sweepstakes for such purposes as I am now covering in this bill.
I have discussed the principle of this bill with that well known public character, the man on the street. In every case I have had an expression of approval, coupled with some surprise that the dominion government does not recognize the absurdity of prohibiting Canadians from holding their own lotteries and the consequent disappearance from Canada of-the money risked by Canadians on such ventures. The average man wants to know why the sale of sweepstake tickets is prohibited, while stock exchanges are allowed to operate and sales on margin are tolerated. Mr. Average Canadian also wants to know why the sale of sweepstake tickets is prohibited, while grain exchanges are in operation where one can trade in grain on margin, and why gambling in mining shares is permitted and betting on race tracks is tolerated. Let us be logical-just logical, but let us be logical. The average Canadian citizen objects to being stamped as a criminal because he risks a few cents in the purchase of a sweepstake ticket, or even shares in the purchase of such a ticket with members of his family or his fellow workers, while anyone can speculate in the stock market, the grain market, the mining market or horse races. He feels that there is hypocrisy about a law of that kind; he buys sweepstake tickets year by year, thereby engaging in transactions prohibited by law, and the profit on those transactions is lost to Canada. Is it to be wondered at that Mr. Average Canadian thinks this prohibition of the sale of sweepstake tickets is foolish, especially when the profits might go to Canadian hospitals? I share his views.
Some hon. members may claim that there are many ways of helping these institutions besides holding sweepstakes. Surely there
Criminal Code-Sweepstakes

are, I agree. Here is a small list of them: raffles, tombolas, dances, bridge parties, soupers d'habitant, soupers du bon vieux temps, strawberry festivals, door-to-door canvass, sales of work, bazaars, kermesses. theatricals, drawings, oyster suppers, pilgrimages, old boy's reunions, euchre parties, bingo'. If hon. members want to know anything more about bingo I advise them to read one of the leading Ottawa papers, Le Droit, and every evening they will see on page 4 an invitation to go to Hull to attend bingo games for the help of a parish. I am not aware that that has been stopped. I was told around Montreal last Sunday that in some parishes they were told not to hold bingo games and bingo games were stopped. Instead of calling them bingo they called them jumbo, and the same thing goes on. In this list I have said nothing of imposts, levies, assessments, rates, taxes and other equally agreeable opportunities of raising money.
There is another element to be considered. Through the adoption of the present bill, by the sale of sweepstake tickets issued under the control of the provincial authorities, these authorities would be able to eliminate the racketeering which we suspect has been going on in the clandestine sale of tickets. We never knew positively whether the sums invested in the sale of sweepstake tickets all reached the management of the sweepstakes. Who could tell whether the tickets offered for sale, bought and sold, were genuine or forgeries? Should the law be amended in accordance with the present bill, the racketeers will not be able to compete with sellers duly authorized and doing business in the open. I have never heard of cut prices in the sale of such tickets, and tickets certainly cannot be adulterated as some other merchandise can be, such as Scotch whisky or other alcoholic liquors for instance.
Speaking of racketeers and racketeering, if hon. members will consult the Montreal papers of Thursday, February 9, 1939, they will read of a seizure of tickets having a face value of $750,000 for the Irish sweepstakes. Think of it, three quarters of a million dollars, 300,000 tickets!
I have received a good deal of fan mail in that connection, containing valuable information as well as divers suggestions. It would be too bad if these were lost to posterity. Among the contributors was L'Union Nationale des Veterans, with head office at 4616 rue Christophe-Colomb, Montreal. They would like a lottery to be organized for granting 
bonuses to veterans under any arrangement fixed by the federal government. They do not object to the principle of lotteries, but would like a dominion law for that purpose. I have not the least objection.
I have also received a proposed plan for monthly sweepstakes in Canada for the benefit of public health services, the first draw to be in Nova Scotia, the second in Prince Edward Island, the third in New Brunswick, the fourth in Quebec, the fifth in Ontario, the sixth in Manitoba, the seventh in Saskatchewan, the eighth in Alberta, the ninth in British Columbia, the tenth in the Yukon, the eleventh in the Northwest Territories and the twelfth for the benefit of the sweepstakes operating costs. I am not going into the details, but I thought hon. members would be interested in knowing about that.
Then I have a letter from a gentleman in Penticton, British Columbia, strongly favouring sweepstakes. He very kindly sent me four newspaper clippings with his letter. I should like to quote these clippings, but will refrain from doing so because they do not indicate their source, and I remember that some weeks ago an hon. member quoted from a newspaper clipping in the afternoon and in the evening it was found that the quotation did not come from the newspaper to which it had been attributed.
In addition to these and many other letters, however, the Financial Post of Toronto was good enough to refer to this bill. Of course I have not the slightest objection to the Financial Post or any other newspaper referring to this matter; very much to the contrary. In its editorial columns of February 4 the Post carried its comment under the heading, "The Sweepstakes Mirage." Again, so far as the title goes, I have no objection, but I do object to the six words at the beginning of the second paragraph: "Apart from questions of public morals-"
If that does not beat the Dutch, the Financial Post talking about public morals because sweepstakes are a mild form of gambling! I ask hon. members what would be the circulation of that same publication if a large part of it were not consecrated to stock gambling. They call it "investing." Of course we must expect some lectures from Toronto on the morality of this matter, since this great city shelters a number of selfappointed keepers of the public morals.
I do not intend to mention every letter I have received, but there is one in particular

Criminal Code-Sweepstakes
which deserves special mention. It comes from Fred Howlett, J.P., city clerk of Vancouver, addressed to myself, and reads:
I beg to notify you of the following resolution which was adopted by the city council on the 13th instant:
"That whereas, on the 24th day of January, 1939, in the House of Commons of Canada, the honourable member for the Jacques-Cartier of Montreal riding, Mr. Mallette, did introduce bill No. 10 entitled an act to amend the criminal code of Canada to legalize sweepstakes, to be organized by, and under the control of the legislature of a province of Canada and the net proceeds of such sweepstakes to be utilized and divided among hospitals and universities;
And whereas such bill did receive its first reading on the 24th day of January, 1939, in the House of Commons;
And whereas the legislative assembly of the province of British Columbia did, on December 9th, 1938, resolve on motion that the said assembly go on record as being in favour of sweepstakes conducted either by the dominion or any provincial government for the benefit of hospitals, which resolution did receive the unanimous approval of the legislative assembly;
And whereas the citizens of Vancouver did express themselves most forcibly when, on December 14th. 1932, by a vote of 25,735 in favour and 9,774 against, they showed themselves in favour of provincially controlled sweepstakes and the net proceeds thereof to be devoted to hospital purposes;
Therefore be it resolved that this council do reaffirm the expressed views of the people of the city of Vancouver and humbly petition parliament to so amend the criminal code of Canada to permit the operation of such sweep-takes for hospital purposes under provincial governmental or municipal control, and that a copy of this resolution be forwarded to all honourable members of the dominion cabinet, to all honourable members of the province of British Columbia, and to the Honourable Mr. Mallette, member of the House of Commons representing Jacques-Cartier riding."
Lotteries are nothing new. Hon. members wishing further information on this important matter are invited to read a book entitled "Lotteries," by H. M. Muller, which can be obtained at the parliamentary library, when I have returned it. At page 22 thereof they will find that lotteries have been organized: first, for facilitating the raising of state loans; second, for reducing the capital of, or interest on, the national debt; third, for raising money for projects not connected with the supply or debt services and, fourth, for raising money as revenue. In 1566-69 Queen Elizabeth authorized by royal proclamation a lottery for improving English harbours and "other publique good workes." The Virginia lotteries of 161215 and 1618-21, for financing the settlement of Virginia, were launched under letters patent. In 1661 the royal fishery lottery was authorized by a proclamation of Charles II, and in 1694 a lottery was authorized by act of parliament. On this continent Harvard college
for a while raised approximately 815,000 a year by lottery and other institutions, such as Dartmouth and William and Mary, raised somewhat lesser amounts by the same device.
A tablet placed on Stoughton Hall, at Harvard, states that it was built in 1805, aided by a state lottery.
I	do not want to make too many references to newspapers, but I should like to quote something which appeared in La Patrie of February 12, signed by Mr. Louis Francoeur who, if I remember correctly, was a candidate of the reconstruction party in the last election:
II	est bien triste pour la province de Quebec qu'elle soit soumise en cette matiere _au pro-hibitionnisme puritain. _ Et l'on continue de s'etonner que Ton fasse ainsi violence 5 l'opinion reflechie de la province, exprimee de la fagon la plus claire possible, par ses parlementaires.
I will translate this roughly as follows:
It is very sad for the province of Quebec to be submitted in this matter to puritan pro-hibitionism, and we continue to be surprised that no account is taken of the considered opinion of this province, expressed in the clearest possible manner by its parliamentarians.
I do not suppose anyone would say money was not needed for education. If there is any doubt about it, let me just remind hon. members that during the last few days we have been swamped with postcards, of which I have some thirty, reading as follows:
Dear Sir:
I am convinced of the vital importance of careful attention being given during the present session of parliament to the need for a national system of university scholarships.
Canadian youth is faced with demoralizing insecurity and it is imperative that the many brilliant matriculating students be permitted to cultivate their exceptional talents. This is important not only from a humanitarian viewpoint but in addition it is indispensable that their potential insights be utilized in the solution of our pressing Canadian problems.
There are few expenditures by our federal government which would be of more value to the whole nation than would be a scholarship grant. Please be assured of my sincere support.
In French we have this, from Montreal students:
(Translation)
Dear Sir,-
Convinced of the need of national scholarships, I beg you to give serious consideration to the matter during the present session.
The complete intellectual development of many gifted young Canadians is impeded by unsurmountable financial obstacles. Permanent scholarships would permit our brilliant young men to devote themselves more effectively to the progress of Canada.
In my opinion, the government could scarcely make a more profitable investment. You may count on my whole-hearted support.
Well, if this question comes before parliament we shall be faced with two things.
Criminal Code-Sweepstakes

In the first place we shall hear that education is a matter for the provinces, which is true; and, second, we shall be asked where the money will come from, because I believe the amount that has been suggested is $500,000. Well, the money will come from the pockets of the ratepayers, as usual, but there is a painless way of getting it; that is through sweepstakes, and I am sure sweepstake tickets for such an end would sell readily. I am convinced that it would be better to keep the money here in Canada than to allow it to either fall into the hands of racketeers or to be exported for the benefit of similar institutions elsewhere.
I have not bothered much with figures; I have spoken simply with regard to the principle involved, because to me it is a question of principle, and I know that those members with whom I have discussed the matter, whether they have been for or against it, also consider it as a matter of principle. I do not know just how much money it will mean, though others have made studies along that line. We know veiy well that such tickets are sold in Canada by the bushel, year in and year out, and that the profits go out of the country. I have tried to explain my point of view, with moderation. I hope it will meet with the approval of at least a majority of hon. members.
