I abide by the ruling of the chair, and shall quote only one or two paragraphs:
The Ottawa Journal, convinced that sweepstakes are an economic vice, would welcome official action that would make the publication of sweepstake winners illegal and close the mails to foreign papers carrying them. Whether the dominion government has power under the present law to enforce such a ban we do not know. Probably it would require an amendment to the criminal code which makes lotteries themselves illegal-with unimportant exceptions. Such a ban certainly would reduce the present illegal sale of lottery tickets, because it would end the display of examples of sudden wealth that lead the unthinking to consider the rare winner and forget the tens of thousands who pay and do not collect.
Then, there is this quotation in the editorial:
"Any state that legalizes lotteries will have a new source of income, but must also be prepared for these consequences:
It will gain a few thousands of dollars at a cost to its people of millions. It will increase its own relief problem. It will encourage new rackets and racketeers. It will not be able to frown upon other forms of gambling. It will do incalculable, harm to the morals of its children and its adult irresponsibles. It will increase public disrespect for government."
I do not need to quote more editorials. Hon. members will recognize the sentiments expressed in them. I might quote from another distinguished paper, namely the Timcs-Journal of Fort William. The editor of that paper is noted for character and ability second to none in Canada. I might also quote from the Port Arthur paper, which of course comes second to that of Fort William. I am sorry the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) is not in the house. I might quote from the Belfast News Letter. In addition to editorials, we know that groups of people throughout Canada have been sending resolutions to members of the house asking us to oppose sweepstakes. Those people are not foolish. They are not people who are out simply to better their own interests. On the contrary they are Christian men and women who believe that sweepstakes would be injurious to Canada.
It has been shown that the hospitals in Dublin have not received very much benefit from sweepstakes, and it is my view that sweepstakes afford a very poor way of raising money for hospitals, universities or anything else.
The biggest business in Canada, namely the churches of this dominion, have more property, more buildings, more directors, more managers, more workers than any other business-and they are better paid. I do not
say they are paid in cash, but they are paid in something that is far ahead of cash. Where is this money for the churches found? It is found in the cottages and the shacks stretched across Canada from Cape Breton to the Pacific coast, from the United States border to the far north. The influence of our churches reaches to every last corner in Canada. How is this money obtained? It is obtained by free-will offerings, by duplex envelopes, by weekly envelopes and other forms of contributions. I may be asked if I have ever been up against it, if I have ever been in need of money. Let me tell hon. members that there has been many a time when I was so straitened for money that I thought of writing to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for a subscription. Then I thought perhaps I had just as much money as he. At least in the words of Ralph Connor, I had just as much money as I could properly take care of and spend.
To those who think we should raise money by sweepstakes, by lotteries and by raffles, let me say that anyone who tries to raise money by that method is slapping the face of the Great Giver who said to us, "Ask and ye shall receive." I should like to tell those who want to raise money for universities and hospitals how to do it. Many hon. members in this house came from the farm, as did I. I know how difficult it was sometimes to get water from the pump in the morning, especially if it was a cold morning. You had to prime the pump, or, as our hired man used to say, you had to soak the sucker. Let me give an example. I heard of a house-to-house canvasser who had been very successful in his work. He was asked to what he attributed his success, and he replied that it depended on the first six words he used when the door was opened. One of his opening remarks when a woman opened the door was, "Madam, is your mother in?" That is an example of priming the pump.
I call to mind that great university in Montreal, the buildings of which are still incomplete. Close by is another beautiful building, that put up by Brother Andre. I ask any hon. member from the province of Quebec: How did Brother Andre raise the money to pay for that place, to keep it in shape and to pay his staff?

How did General Booth raise the necessary money to keep the Salvation Army going? That was raised by voluntary subscriptions, by showing people men who were down and out, women who had gone to the devil. He showed the world the work of the Salvation Army, and he was able to get support all over the country. How do we get our money? I think of one man connected with our own church in the city of Toronto. He would make a fine minister of finance and he would carry out that work with the greatest dignity. He would know where every dollar came from, and where every dollar went to. That is a good characteristic for any minister of finance to have. That man is capable of handling large amounts of money. He knows where the need is, he sees what work must be done, and then he gets the money.
What do we need more than money? What do we need more than taxes? We need moral rearmament against the things that are spoiling us, with which we are all familiar. My

time seems to be passing faster than usual to-night. I gave three reasons last year why I was opposed to this resolution and, like a youth, they seem to have grown since that time. A system of sweepstakes would be bad economics. The great concern of all sensible people to-day is the creation without violence of a sound economic order. The basis of such an order must be sought in wise planning, general productivity and a reasonable distribution of the goods produced. It is utterly impossible to build a sound economic order on anything which has the semblance of gambling. It kindles the adventurous spirit in men, it detaches them from their daily tasks and creates a fraternity of men who are not, in any real sense, of value economically. The late Ramsay MacDonald said that gambling is marked by an impatience with the slow process of legitimate accumulation and by a revolt against the discipline of steady growth and sustained action. Any one who wishes to understand must realize that when you spend $2.50 to buy a sweepstake ticket, you cannot hope to see anything come back. There may be a very, very slight hope, but it is 400,000 times deferred. Therefore, I say it is bad economics.
I should like to give the house just a word along this line from another source to show that it is bad economics. In France they tried sweepstakes for five years, and at the end of that time they withdrew them, for at least two reasons. One was that 3 J per cent only of the sweepstakes went to the purpose for which they were collected; 96J per cent of the money raised by lottery went some other place. The French chamber of deputies saw that the boys and girls of France were being exploited; they were being used by racketeers. Therefore, they said, lotteries were not fair to the young people of France, and those lotteries, which at one time seemed to have a fine prospect of making good, have been withdrawn. Why are there not lotteries in the United States to-day? They have been withdrawn long since; the last one was in Louisiana in 1894. Why was it abolished? Because the odour of those sweepstakes became so obnoxious to the better people of the United States that they could be tolerated no longer.
I said last year that you do not find any Hebrews buying sweepstakes, because they know what good business is and what bad business is. You do not find many Scotchmen buying sweepstakes, because they see it is bad business.

I should like to state the opinion of our general council in 1938:
The general council reaffirmed its opposition to gambling in any form-"whether in stocks, wheat, at the race course, the card table, in connection with sport, lotteries or raffles," and especially deplored resort to gambling devices to secure funds for religious or benevolent purposes. It expressed the opinion that gambling carnivals sponsored by service clubs and other organizations have an injurious effect upon public morals and are especially harmful to the mind of youth.
That may not be popular doctrine. All sane people welcome a bit of fun. I like a bit of fun, and I like to see a good, clean game. Unless something important is in progress on Thursday night, I might go with some other hon. members to a fine game of hockey, because I believe that "all work and no play makes Jack a dull boy." You must have fun; but fun must be clean, it must be out in the open, and it must be in keeping with the plea that you, Mr. Speaker, put before this house every day.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMISSION WITH POWERS OF ADMINISTRATION AND CONTROL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support this bill, with which I agree in general although I take exception to some of the clauses in it. The bill is at least broad enough to include many things, under the operation of the commission which will be the resultant creature from this bill, that are at least new to Canadian life.
Prison reform cannot take place in a day. A hundred years ago there were scores of offences for which a man could be hanged. That is not the case now. I think we have learned over a period of years to differentiate between several things; first of all, to differentiate between the anti-social mind and the criminal mind. We have learned to differentiate between punishment as a deterrent to crime and punishment as fitting the criminal to be punished. I would not say that Canada lags behind the rest of the world in penitentiary reform, for the reason that there has been evolved no right way to punish crime, no right way to deter a criminal, no right way to rehabilitate a criminal, no right way to prevent crime.
I would say, however, that we in Canada have been backward in making any effort toward solution, and I believe that this bill may be the means of our progressing as a nation towards penitentiary reform. Furthermore, I see no reason why Canada cannot lead the way. Up through the years governments have been hampered by well-meaning though uninformed, I will not say unintelligent, people. Unbridled sentimentalism born of pity, the stirring up of the emotions, the heart speaking loudly and the brain and mind not at all, have created plenty of mischief in the way of penitentiary reform.
There must be no mollycoddling of prisoners, and any action we take must not of necessity be from the sympathetic point of view but must be from the point of view of common sense. The real case against the prison system is that it is not effective. It is unproductive of results rather than necessarily too humane. Until recent years the penitentiary systems at large in Canada were, I believe, cruel. I do not think any member of this house or any Canadian would care to see us go back to the nineteenth century, when the deterrence of crime occupied such a large place in the minds of people, when very, very cruel and long sentences were

imposed. Therefore it is quite natural to expect that research along the improvement of penitentiary control should be logically along humane lines. But our penitentiary system stands or falls, is a success or a failure, according to its effectiveness. The only rational alternative is a prison system that is directed towards making those who go to prison come out better men than when they went there, and with all our reforms we are still very far from that goal in Canada. But I would say that this bill may be the basis of broad treatment toward success.
There are to be appointed three commissioners and perhaps three deputy commissioners, the commission having power to add to their number; and if the commission fails to make a study, first, of crime prevention and, second, of the rehabilitation of the prisoner, with a reasonable amount of aftercare, then it will not have achieved the end that is possible. Such changes as will make our prisons real centres for the training of the law-breaker in social responsibility constitute the need.
The bill provides for the establishment of a commission to control the penitentiaries. I submit that their duties under this legislation can very well be widened to take care of those two phases of crime that I have mentioned. As regards crime prevention, they might act perhaps through the family court, the juvenile court; and the rehabilitation of prisoners should start first of all within the walls of the penitentiary and then outside.
I was surprised to learn, though I need not have been, that the family court, that timely and valuable innovation in Canadian law and justice, had its beginning in the city of Ottawa right within a stone's throw of this chamber- and when I say a stone's throw I am visualizing a throw by Babe Ruth rather than a throw by the hon. member for Hamilton West, because I could not throw so far. I have said that Canada can lead the world in penitentiary reform, and in view of the fact that the family court started in Ontario I think I can reiterate that statement.
A few days ago when this bill was in the resolution stage the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. McCann) made an observation, quoting from the report of the royal commission from which this bill has been evolved. He stated that 1S8 prisoners, repeating criminals, recidivists, in Canada had cost the dominion $4,500,000 or $25,000 per criminal.
I suggested that, in view of this, crime prevention has a real place in the activities of this commission, and that $4,500,000 would go a

long way toward such. It would be a case of a stitch in time saving nine, to quote an old, hackneyed truism.

speechtext:
I was going to say that
the hon. member will not disturb me at any time if he quotes from the good book. The responsibility of parents in the home is a real thing in Canadian life to-day, and we as parents are not living up to that responsibility. It has been said from platform and pulpit-and I was guilty of saying the same thing myself not many weeks ago-that the church has failed. I did not mean to say that the church has failed, but we as church members have failed to live up to our obligations to the church. Our municipalities have been quickened in the last two decades in their responsibility towards the youth of our cities. They have opened recreation places and playgrounds; they have built beautiful parks in order that our children may be taken off the streets.
The churches on the other hand have fully lived up to their responsibilities. The church has socialized itself to meet physical as well as spiritual need. It has taken the boys and girls off the streets and put them in church gymnasiums where they have opportunities to play basketball, badminton and other worth while games good for body and mind. But we as parents have neglected the training of children in the homes; we have neglected the family altar and have not lived up to the heritage which is ours, the opportunity to teach -the youngsters how to live, to get along with their neighbours and to take a place in life. In that connection I should like to quote from the annual report upon prisons and reformatories, 1936, over the signature of the Hon. Harry Nixon. In that report it is stated:
It is quite evident that many parents are not successfully training their children and the many organizations engaged in working among and assisting the youth of the province have not been entirely able to counterbalance the evident deficiency in home training.
With that idea in mind I should like to draw a' comparison in respect to crime between times of affluence and times of depression. It has been said that crime increases in times of distress, that depressions create crime. On that I should like to give a few figures. In 1930 -there were in Ontario 3,366,000 people. The number committed for trial in that year was 29,126. There were 21,421 persons sentenced to prison. That was in a year of great prosperity, when everyone had money, when conditions were easier, when it was easy to make a living. In the depression years of 1931, 1932, 1933, 1934, we find the population of Ontario increasing, but the number of persons committed for trial dropped steadily and those sentenced to prison became fewer and fewer. The following are the figures for persons sentenced to prison for those years:
1931		 18,127
1932		 15,804
1933		 14,538
1934		 13,509
Meanwhile the population of Ontario increased and business became worse. So it is not true to say that crime is less in times of prosperity and increases in -times of distress. But despite the fact that fewer young men and young women, as well as older men and women, were working; despite the fact that our service clubs, churches, municipalities were doing everything in their power to take boys and girls off the streets, the home did not keep pace. The sanctity of the home must find a real place in the life of our nation.
1654	COMMONS
Penitentiaries Commission-Mr. Marsh
I point out that modem city life intensifies opportunities for friction and crime. It increases the need for regulatory laws as well as opportunities for their evasion. Not only do these things make for increased lawlessness, but the irritation they cause also tends to reduce respect for law, which many still attribute to some mysterious ethical organ in the soul of man, but which in fact is the result of complex conditioning factors. City life tends to sharpen and dramatize economic inequalities. Side by side with the luxuries displayed * in shop windows, crowded slum dwellings make wholesome life exceedingly hard to maintain, children seek the streets, gang life is stimulated. The rewards of urban criminality are very much greater than they were when you, sir, and I were boys. There is ten times the temptation for youth to-day than there was in our boyhood. Not for a moment would I criticize our merchants for their manner of displaying merchandise, or say that they should change it, but I instance the counter of the five, ten and fifteen cent stores where merchandise is displayed attractively to excite longings in the minds of boys and girls. It is really wonderful to me that our boys and girls are as honest as they are.
Let me now say a word or two about the rehabilitation of criminals. If rehabilitation and aftercare are not undertaken, the majority of imprisoned offenders will again find their way back to prison. From an economic standpoint it would be cheaper to keep habitual criminals in prison than to let them out to break the law again, be brought again before the bar of justice, be prosecuted and defended by lawyers at the cost of the taxpayer. Nevertheless we cannot sentence a man to life imprisonment for an offence not calling for that sentence. It is cheaper still to cure criminals, if it is possible to do so. If methods of prevention fail, treatment in prison should be directed towards correcting the anti-social or criminal viewpoint. I have not quite made up my mind whether men and women are more susceptible to heart appeals than to appeals to the pocketbook; but whether we regard this matter from the point of view of humanity and justice or the materialistic viewpoint of dollars and cents, we must come to the same conclusion, that care must be given to the rehabilitation of the ex-criminal.
I think it is natural for all of us, as the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) brought out quite clearly this afternoon, to be more concerned about finding jobs for the lawkeeper than the lawbreaker. That is human nature, and we shall probably continue

to feel that way; but I submit-and here I hark back to the holy book-that this was exactly the point of view of the elder brother of the prodigal son, and it was not the right point of view. Strongly as we feel that we must work for the young fellow who observes the law, we must not be oblivious to the need for rehabilitation of the criminal from the viewpoint either of the pocketbook or of the man himself. The graduate from a penitentiary finds it doubly hard to get employment for the following reasons:	First,
he has been out of touch with world events and the progress of society, so that sooner or later he will disclose the fact that he has been absent from society for a prolonged period. Second, he has become accustomed to irresponsibility, has been told what to do, lias been fed, clothed, relieved of the responsibilities of life, and therefore he is not fit to take his place in an employment line-up and get himself a job. Third, sooner or later it becomes known that he is an ex-convict. Even if his employer is willing to keep him, other employees probably go to the employer and say, "We will not work with that man;" consequently he' loses his job. Here a process of education of the man on the street must be followed. Canadians must be made to realize that not only should they help in restoring that man to civil life, but if they do not, they as Canadian taxpayers are paying to keep that man in an institution. Fourth, competition is too keen in the labour market for anybody but a skilled tradesman to get employment. It may so happen that within the penitentiary walls a convict has been trained to take his place with the best of artisans, but in the main he is less well fitted to take a job. Fifth, ex-convicts have insufficient resources to keep them over the long period which is often necessary before they can secure work. Sixth, ex-convicts cannot afford to be homeless, because if they are picked up by the police for vagrancy their record stands against them. Further, the public generally will not accept them into society.
What does after-care consist of? As soon as a man has been convicted and before he is sentenced, his case should be looked into by the representative of the commission for that district, who has followed the trial, so that knowledge of the cause of his criminal action may be of aid to the judge in passing sentence. At any rate the data thus obtained should be available to the penitentiary warden, for three reasons: One, it will help the warden to determine the trade for which the prisoner is fitted; two, it will aid the warden in deter-

Penitentiaries Commission-Mr. Marsh
mining the type and amount of discipline that he needs to fit him for civil life again, and the means whereby his anti-social tendencies may be corrected. Then, of course, his mental and physical condition should be reported upon. Based upon this data, the prison authorities should plan that man's path back into society; the start should be made within the penitentiary walls and continued through an agency or a person appointed by the commission. The cost of after-care is less than the cost of the repeating criminal, the recidivist, and there will be no further cost from the criminal activities of the man who becomes rehabilitated. He will become a producer, a contributor to society, instead of a non-producer and a liability.
I should like now to say a word about the parole system and the system of remission. I think the remission board definitely and entirely should be under the direction of the penitentiary commission. I do not think there is any room whatever for dual control in that regard, and I do believe the parole system and the indeterminate sentence, as practised in Ontario, should receive the attention of the dominion government and of this commission. In Ontario ninety per cent of those paroled successfully completed their parole and were absorbed into private life without further offending the law. I would also direct the minister's attention to the fact that in Ontario two prisons have been closed, largely as a result of the parole system and the indeterminate sentence. In Ontario a man cannot be released on parole unless he has a job awaiting him. How long does he keep that job? Well, recently a check was made of those paroled within the previous eighteen months, and ninety per cent of them were found still working at their jobs. That is accounted for by the fact that the relatives and friends of that man do their best to rehabilitate him into civil life. He comes out of prison with' a job to go to, and it is the particular care of these people that he be kept at work. They play big brother to him; they open up avenues that otherwise would be closed to him, and I suggest that we might well take advantage of this agency.
In that connection I should like to quote from the report on the prisons and reformatories of Ontario which I hold in my hand, over the signature of the Hon. Harry Nixon, provincial secretary. According to this report, in 1935-36 the parole board held forty-five meetings, investigated 2,339 cases and authorized parole in 1,421 cases. There were 1,067 paroles put into effect; eleven prisoners were recommended for deportation; twentyfour disappeared while on parole; seventy committed crimes while on parole and were reconvicted, while seventeen were returned to reformatory, their paroles cancelled. So it will be seen that in almost 1,200 cases paroles were granted, and only 111 failed to make good. Of those 111, some seventy were reconvicted of crimes and returned to gaol, so they were not turned loose upon society to commit further crimes. This report goes on to make this comment:
Many of these prisoners paroled are heads of families, and too often with the breadwinner in custody the family must be dependent on charity or public relief. By the one process of granting parole the family is likely to become self-supporting and the province is saved the cost of maintaining the prisoner in the institution.
I have investigated many of these parole cases and have found that in some instances years after the man has served his sentence, years after he has been reinstated in private life, he has returned to his parole officer for advice, guidance and counsel, which speaks well for the personal element, the humanitarian element that enters into this problem.
I should like to say a word also with regard to the parole and probation system as it is operated in Hamilton under Magistrate Harry Burbidge, who has made a special study of this question and has been signally successful. The parole and probation system has worked out very well, probably because in some degree Magistrate Burbidge punishes those who break parole.	[DOT]
We must not, of course, lose sight of the fact that we have in our penitentiaries incurables who are a menace to society, who must be watched closely after they have served their sentences. There are also those who should suffer lifelong incarceration, but that does not excuse us from paying attention to those who may be rehabilitated. It must be borne in mind that 188 recidivists cost this country $4,500,000, or $25,000 each, so from the viewpoint of economy as well as the viewpoint of common sense and humanitarian-ism we must pay attention to the rehabilitation of the criminal.
To sum up very briefly what I have said, Mr. Speaker, in the first place the penitentiaries commission to be created under this act should include among its duties: first, penitentiary reform based on constructive rather than sympathetic grounds; second, the study,, of the family court, of juvenile delinquency and crime prevention; third, the rehabilitation of the criminal, including probation and parole along national lines; fourth, more intelligent study and treatment of

chronic alcoholics. I would ask the minister and hon. members this: When a chronic alcoholic offends against the law, what do we do with him? We put him either in gaol or in an insane asylum. That is not right. He is not a criminal; he is anti-social, and some special provision should be made for his case. I am speaking, of course, of the apparently incurable alcoholic.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, we should have the absolute removal of penitentiaries administration from party patronage and politics. This afternoon the minister assured us that this was to become a reality. I just wanted to add my humble contribution to the discussion on this bill. What I am most interested in is the treatment accorded the officers and employees of the penitentiaries in Canada. That does not mean, of course, that I am not interested in the welfare of the prisoners, because afteT all they are human beings who have had the misfortune to commit what we call crimes. I am one of those who believe that in the treatment of prisoners we should apply the laws of psychology. I sincerely believe that in these days, when there are wonderful developments of science, there should be a way of bringing these citizens back on the right path, by the application of the law of psychology. I have witnessed the cure of the bad habits of children when, while they have been sleeping, right thoughts have been introduced to their minds, and that procedure has had the effect of correcting wrong habits which, according to common knowledge, had followed them from birth.
I believe the same laws should apply to prisoners. While I am expressing my views with respect to the treatment of criminals and the possibility of bringing them back to civil life, I take occasion to congratulate the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Marsh) upon his well prepared observations. I am deeply interested in the treatment accorded officers and guards of the penitentiaries. I find at page 353 of the report of the commission a recommendation that the pay of officers be brought up to a reasonable level, having regard to the type of service performed. We find that section 11 of the bill states that:
The commission may appoint such guards, trade instructors and other subordinate officers, employees and servants as are necessary for the service of any of the penitentiaries.

Subsection 2 is in these words:
The guards, trade instructors and other officers, employees and servants so appointed shall be paid such salaries as are approved by the governor in council.
I am pleased to see that provision in the measure. It does not imply that the guards and other officers were ill-treated, but I am under the impression that some improvement will be highly appreciated. Nevertheless I do not see anything in the recommendations with respect to the hours of labour of guards. If my information is correct, the guards are on continuous duty for twelve consecutive hours. I do not believe that a guard who performs such strenuous and tiresome work, and who must shoulder the responsibilities they have to carry, should be bound to work that length of time consecutively. I believe the recommendation of the international labour office with respect to the eight-hour day should be in force in penitentiaries as it is in other fields of activity.
I am sure the body which will be responsible for the administration of penitentiaries in Canada will attempt to improve the situation of officers and guards in the same way as they are going to improve their wages. I am satisfied that this action will be taken when, under this measure, the commission is appointed.

In the arrest, trial and imprisonment of the two would-be robber brothers, Owen and Gordon McNeil, I feel it to be a profound sense of duty to protest strongly the judgment meted out to them.
It is only about three years ago that I saw these lads almost daily going to and from the public school, happy and care-free. On Sunday afternoons they attended my Sunday school and my Sunday school superintendent with me taught the lesson and the divine principles upon which

Christian character is founded. These two boys were always timid and shy, reserved, intellectually subnormal through no fault of their own.

Mr. Speaker, I think it would be too bad to let this bill pass without saying a word or two of praise for some of those who pioneered in introducing the prison reform question in this house. The hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail) gave a great deal of study to this question, and she did a great deal of travelling in order to investigate different institutions. She made her own investigations and presented her findings to the house. I believe the late Harry Anderson, a former editor of the Toronto Globe, rendered perhaps the greatest assistance outside the house in bringing about the results which we hope will accrue from the bill introduced by the minister. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has always been a staunch advocate of prison reform. I think the house should give credit to the three persons I have mentioned, as well as to others whom I have not mentioned but who have rendered assistance in this effort.
I only have a few observations to make. The greatest reform which should be the objective of any bill of this type is to keep people out of prison. But a bill, of course, cannot do that. Folks go to prison for several reasons. Perhaps the first main reason springs from the impossible homes that some children are ushered into. Those who give part of

Penitentiaries Commission-Mr. MacNicol
their time to surveying what it is that misdirects children find frequently that some homes are simply impossible. Some parents themselves take no interest whatever in their children. I am not going to elaborate upon what can be done in that regard. Economic conditions are another reason why so many have to go to a place of detention. Perhaps another cause is lack of opportunity for sports. In the last few years a great advance in that regard has been made in Canada, but still too many hundreds and thousands of children are compelled to play on the streets instead of having some better place of recreation. There are many parks, but not sufficient. Perhaps more along that line might help to decrease the prison population. Those who have travelled in the old land know that all over that country there are great commons. One day I went to one outside London. I am sure there must have been fifty to seventy-five thousand young people, girls and boys, who had gone there over the holiday, taking their bicycles and tents, and were staying there a day or two. In Canada we have nothing of that kind. There is hardly any place for one to park outside the cities. If one takes his car outside Toronto and parks alongside some farm, he is frequently ordered away. There is no place where a man could slip over the fence and find accommodation such as is provided on the commons of England.
The second main objective should be to eliminate the repeater. I believe the minister has that object in view. Particularly do I believe that because of his being so strong for the Borstal system. I made a fairly exhaustive investigation into the operation of the Borstal system in the old country. I have in mind one prison where it was being operated. When I was there, three or four offenders came up to the gate. The man at the gate is not in uniform. One young lad came up with his head in the air and his hat on the back of his head, in a spirit of bravado. Another seemed to be dejected. But no matter what their demeanour was, the man inside the gate would at once start to treat them as though he were their father.
After they were a number of hours in the prison I was amazed at the fashion in which they were treated. They begin at once to teach them to "play the game," and all through their prison life they are taught not to let the prison down. If they come back again, of course, they let the prison down. In their sports the prisoners themselves put the younger lads through their paces. They drill them and train them. If one young lad is out of step or does not move lively or
quickly, the prisoner who is training him tells him, "Now, don't let your squad down; stick up for your squad; you are competing against another squad." They are always reminding them not to let their fellows down, with the final purpose that they shall understand before they leave for the world again that they must not let their prison down. They are lined up in all sorts of teams and play, not only inside but outside the prison walls.
After they have been there for a while they are trusted and put upon their honour not to let the prison down. About seven miles from Wakefield is a three hundred acre farm. When a first offender is approaching the limit of his detention period, he is sent to that farm with others who are in a like position. There they are under supervision, mostly of other prisoners, with only a few guards. They are put on their honour to go to work away from the prison on this big farm, not even returning to the prison at night, and if they have proved that they are faithful to their prison and not likely to let it down, when their time comes they go away quite happily.
Another prison had a very large farm forty miles distant. Here again the supervision was mostly by other prisoners, with only a few guards in attendance. That is part of the Borstal system. They had gymnasia, and to my amazement the deputy warden himself was wrestling and boxing with a number of the prisoners. I saw no firearms anywhere, and no attempt to cow or submerge the prisoners. At all times they were being taught to try to recover their manhood and not to let down the institution from which they would before long return to society.
I have just one further word to say. In 1936 there were 8,462 male prisoners in the prisons of the old land. Of these 688 had been Borstal boys. That is a very small number out of the total, approximately 13,300, that had been trained in the Borstal prisons from the inception of the system in 1908 or thereabouts. It represents only about 5-1 per cent. The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Marsh) referred to the good results we are getting in Ontario from the parole system, and mentioned that only about ten per cent had failed. Well, according to these figures, only 5T per cent of those whom the Borstal system has tried to rehabilitate have failed.
In conclusion, let me say that I have every confidence in the minister. As long as he holds his office I will support him as well as I can towards realizing the objective he has in view.

I do not purpose delaying the passage of this bill through its third reading, but as I did not delay it at all in its second or first reading perhaps I might be permitted just a word here.
We are told in the explanatory notes that the general object of this bill is to establish a commission with power under the Minister of Justice to control and manage the penitentiaries. That is a tall order. We fully realize that as a result of the conditions of the past ten years many are inhabiting our penal institutions who would never have been incarcerated but for the circumstances under which they have been compelled to live, very often through no fault of their own.
To control and manage a penitentiary is one thing, and to control and manage or attempt to have some part in managing the future lives of those who are the inmates of that penitentiary is another. So it evolves that the commission which will be set up under this bill has given to it a serious and grave responsibility. The bill of itself is not perfect. There are phases of it which some of us would like to see slightly altered. On the other hand, in the main it is good. The report of the royal commission to investigate our penal institutions is full of recommendations, many of which are good; and as I understand it from the minister, the now commission is to consider the report of the royal commission and govern itself upon the recommendations as it sees fit.
The report of the royal commission itself had its genesis many years ago, and society in Canada owes a debt of gratitude to the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Macphail) for her excellent work in making this report possible.
Those of us who, as a result of our vocations or even avocations outside this house, have dealt with youth for the past twenty years, realize that one of the most important phases in connection with our penal institutions is the way in which the young lad is let out. He may have the advantage of being placed in one of the better penitentiaries; but after all, when he leaves, he is still in the minds of many an outcast from society. He finds it extraordinarily difficult to become reestablished, and if it so happens that the crime for which he has been put in gaol was committed in a location far removed from his home, if he had one, he is sent back to that place from which he was committed to prison, and left to drift. As a result of the interest which many sterling men and women have taken in these young men, legion is the name of those who have been reclaimed for society. But in great part this has been, not because of the penitentiary in which they were placed

but in spite of it. Therefore it seems to me that one of the most important jobs that this commission has to perform is to see to it not only that it controls and manages the penitentiaries, but that it makes sure that when the man is released there are agencies as far as possible to look after his future to the fullest and best end.
I shall watch with a great deal of interest the progress which this commission makes, because my interest in this whole matter is exceedingly keen. I sincerely hope, as does the whole of Canada, that the minister will exercise that rare judgment of his in the appointment of this commission and make sure beyond any possible doubt that there cannot be even any suspicion of a political tinge in the choice of those who become its members. If there is any matter in this dominion that cuts across party lines, it is the one that we are now considering; and I am fully confident, knowing the minister as I do, that he will make sure that the commission is not handicapped at the outset by the stigma of partisanship.
There is much that I should like to say at this point. I may associate myself fully with the remarks so ably made to-night by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Marsh), and, as I have said, I shall watch with much interest and expectation the progress of the commission.

MACPHAIL (Grey-Bruce): I am sure the passage of this bill will please the minister, but before it carries I wish to say how much I appreciate the gracious words of the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNieol) and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey). The purpose of the bill which is to be founded on this resolution is fairly, if briefly, described in the resolution itself, but I might add something to acquaint the committee with the purposes of the bill. Perhaps primarily the reason for the framing of the bill is the fact that the film has become a very important and powerful factor in the dissemination of information, the production of entertainment, and for publicity purposes generally and it is growing constantly. Various departments of the government-I need not
mention them particularly, but at least five or six departments of the government-have had in the past their own film activities entirely independent of one another. It must be evident that the matter of films has advanced to the stage where it may be often in the national interest to prepare films which will serve national purposes as distinct from those of any individual department.
As I have stated, various departments have been preparing their own films-and this is not a criticism of any department-but the preparation of these films has been conducted in a more or less haphazard way, no one department cooperating with another, with the result that there has been a good deal of overlapping, consequent lack of economy, and also of efficiency. Believing that, the government feel that it would be a step in the right direction to coordinate the various film activities of the different departments by creating what is called in the bill a national film board, which shall have control of the film activities of the various departments of government, not entirely assuming their responsibilities, because each department will still have power to initiate its own films, but these films will be approved by the central board.
